summary: SIP lets calls, messages and other requests reach a person without their explicit consent, which can enable spam and denial-of-service attacks. This document lists requirements for SIP extensions that add consent-based communication. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Today anyone can ring your doorbell. This note says there should be a way for you to say who is allowed to, so pranksters get turned away.

questions: what is consent based communication in sip
how do sip amplification attacks work
what are the sip consent requirements
subtitle: Why SIP needs a way for people to say who may send them requests, and what such a system must do.

tldr.problem: In SIP, anyone can send a request to any user, and servers that relay requests can be abused to flood a target or to deliver spam, with no consent from the recipient.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 17 requirements (REQ 1 to REQ 17) that a consent framework for SIP must meet, starting with the rule that relays must not deliver a request unless the recipient has granted them permission.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol itself. It is a requirements document that later SIP extensions for consent-based communication were expected to satisfy.

today: RFC 4453 is an Informational document. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it defines requirements rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
SIP carries many kinds of communication: audio, video, text, instant messaging and presence. A sender starts one by transmitting a request such as INVITE or MESSAGE to the recipient. The recipient can reject it, but the SIP network delivers it without the recipient's explicit consent.

The document says this open model can cause problems, including amplification attacks, and that these problems have plagued email. At the time of writing most SIP services were not interconnected, so such attacks were rare compared with email. The SIPPING working group wanted to address them proactively, before they became as burdensome as they are for email.

The RFC does two things: it explains the problems of SIP's open design, and it defines requirements for adding a consent framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who knows your address can knock on your door, and you only get to say no after the knock. The writers wanted to fix this before it became a big nuisance, like junk email.

sections.title: The Problem: Open Delivery and Amplification
sections.content:
In networks built on RFC 3261 and RFC 3263, anyone can address a request to any SIP user by using that user's SIP URI, and the network will usually deliver it. Call screening can block requests, but it is not widespread and is not a systematic solution. When a request arrives, the user agent typically alerts the user, for example by ringing or opening a pop-up window. For MESSAGE requests the content is usually shown to the user.

SUBSCRIBE is different. Those requests are normally handled by network-based state agents, and the watcher information event package lets a user approve or deny them. So presence already works on consent. That mechanism does not, however, protect network agents against denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.

The main danger is amplification. Proxies can fork one request to several contacts, and SIP URI-list services send a new copy of a request to every entry in a list. A user could build a resource list of 100 entries, each of the form sip:identifier@target-IP. One SUBSCRIBE sent to that list makes the server generate 100 requests aimed at the target, which does not even need to be a SIP node. The target addresses can differ and still hit one machine, for instance all in one subnetwork, where the access router becomes the victim.

The same amplifiers can deliver spam. For INVITE that looks like telemarketer calls; for MESSAGE it can be a never-ending stream of pop-ups with unwanted content.

The framework for SIP URI-list services already mandates opt-in lists, which are one form of consent-based communication.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a copy machine that anyone can load with one letter and a list of 100 addresses. A prankster could make it mail 100 copies to one poor house. Asking the house owner first would stop that.

sections.title: The Seventeen Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC defines a relay as any SIP server (proxy, back-to-back user agent or a hybrid) that receives a request and translates the request URI into one or more next-hop URIs to which it delivers a request. The requirements apply to solutions for consent in such relays.

The core rules are these. REQ 1: the solution must keep relays from delivering a request unless the recipient has explicitly granted permission to the relay using appropriately authenticated messages. REQ 2: relays must not generate more than one outbound request per inbound request unless the target resource has granted permission, so that the consent mechanism does not itself become a DoS target.

Permissions have to be flexible. They must be able to name a specific user by Address-of-Record (REQ 3), be set separately for each SIP service that forwards to the recipient (REQ 4, for example allowing domain A but not domain B), and be revocable at any time (REQ 5). Revoking must not require the user or user agent to store information (REQ 6).

Scope and reach: the solution must work between domains without pre-established relationships (REQ 7), for all current and future SIP methods (REQ 8), for forking proxies (REQ 9), and for URI-list services such as resource list servers, MESSAGE URI-list services and dial-out conference servers (REQ 10). It must work whether a URI list is stored on the server or carried in the request (REQ 11).

Further rules cover privacy and robustness. Anonymous communication is allowed if the recipient accepts it (REQ 12), and a recipient can grant permission without the sender learning who it is (REQ 13). The system must not be foolable into delivering a request for which permission was not granted (REQ 14). Neither side has to be online when the other acts: the recipient need not be connected when communication is attempted (REQ 15), and the sender need not be connected when permission is given (REQ 16). Finally, the solution should scale to Internet-wide deployment (REQ 17).
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: the helper must ask first, must not make extra copies without leave, and you must be able to change your mind any time. It must work between strangers, even when you are offline, and it must not be easy to trick.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is a single sentence: security has been discussed throughout the document. The whole document is about protecting SIP users and network agents from spam and denial-of-service abuse, so the requirements above are themselves the security content.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole note is about keeping pranksters out, so there is no separate chapter saying so.
